title: Something to cluck about: America’s backyard chicken boom
text:
Something to cluck about: America’s backyard chicken boom
Americans are flocking to small-time egg suppliers, drawn by fresher, more humane food – and a yearning for simpler, more local living.
On any given day, while America’s giant automated farms roll out more than 200 million eggs, Neil and Paul Couvee walk through henhouses, collecting their harvest by hand. They grade, wash, and pack it on-site. By the next morning, nearly 4,000 fresh eggs will be for sale in their Bedford, Massachusetts, store, not 50 feet from the barn.
Never mind that it’s far more work- and time-intensive to produce and sell these eggs. Or that Chip-in Farm’s prices are nearly triple those at the grocery store. A happy, old-fashioned spirit infuses the place and draws a steady stream of customers. “It’s more humane,” says Hilary Taylor, a jewelry silversmith in nearby Carlisle, who arrived one morning for a fresh dozen. The eggs “are fresher. They haven’t traveled.”
“I have been coming here for years,” says another woman, holding a bag of purchases in one hand and her granddaughter’s hand in the other. The granddaughter adds: “The chickens make the eggs, so they are fresh. Cluck, cluck.”
For Thanksgiving, the Monitor takes a closer look at the ingredients in pumpkin pie, including pumpkins, eggs, and flour, to discover what stories they might hold. Our economics reporter found Americans are flocking to small-time egg suppliers, drawn by fresher, more humane food.
Increasingly, people are making efforts to return to food raised the way their grandparents or great-grandparents were used to. They buy vegetables, meat, and eggs from small-scale, local farms, some certified organic. Or they raise it themselves on small plots of land. And if they want to keep livestock, egg-laying chickens are often a relatively easy – and less expensive – way to start.
“The way we are doing this is coming back,” says Neil Couvee.
Egg and flow
In the case of chickens, the move toward backyard coops began in the 1990s but has taken off within the past decade, nearly doubling from about 5.8 million U.S. households in 2018 to roughly 13 million households (or roughly 5% of total) by early 2025. Chickens have even become popular as pets.
So this Thanksgiving, when Americans dig into the stuffing, rolls, sweet potato casserole, pecan pies, and other holiday favorites, many will know the origin of the eggs that helped make those dishes. Some may even know the names of the chickens that hatched them.
Laying groundwork
Two events in recent years temporarily pushed the movement into overdrive.
In 2020, the pandemic kept many people at home, giving them time and opportunity to improve their houses and yards. Some chose to buy egg-laying chickens and build coops to house them. Then last year, the bird flu crisis prompted the culling of millions of chickens at both commercial and smaller operations. In some places, eggs ran short. And prices tripled, peaking at a national average of $6.23 a dozen.
“We were cheaper than some of the supermarkets,” recalls Jodi Mahoney, store manager of Chip-in Farm. “We had to limit the number of eggs people could buy.”
The combination of higher egg prices and shortages caused even more consumers to turn to backyard farming. Orders for chicks and coops skyrocketed. One Midwest hatchery reported that in 2025, it presold 40 weeks’ worth of chicks, where a normal backlog was two or three.
The commercial egg industry has since recovered, and prices have returned to normal levels. (In September, the national average price stood at $2.27 a dozen.) That has cooled interest in backyard production. Iowa’s Murray McMurray Hatchery’s backlog, for example, has fallen from 40 weeks last year to 10 weeks. Missouri’s Cackle Hatchery reports that sales are down 20%.
“If you’re just trying to save money, you’re not going to do that” by raising backyard chickens, says Jeff Smith, third-generation owner and CEO of Cackle. Even without counting startup costs, the feed alone is often worth more than eggs produced.
Coop-ing it cool
“It’s more for the calming of the spirit,” Mr. Smith says. It’s “learning how to take care of animals and knowing what you’re eating, and being self-reliant. If those are the things you want, then definitely I think that’s the way you need to go.”
Some backyard chicken families have stopped replenishing their stock, deciding to make a slow exit from the business. Mark Guetersloh, a part-time Chip-in employee, is one of them. “I raised $75 eggs,” he jokes. He began keeping chickens because of his son’s interest, but now that his son has left home, the family is winding down its flock.
Still, new entrants keep coming in.
“Once people have an established family, that’s typically when they want to get into it,” says Matt Bradley, marketing director for Hoover’s Hatchery in Rudd, Iowa.
Even if people get into it for the eggs, they sometimes keep doing it for the chickens.
“There’s a lot of people who have also found a lot of, maybe, entertainment and enjoyment” in their chickens, says David Anderson, a professor and extension economist for livestock and food product marketing at Texas A&M University in College Station. One friend “has the Taj Mahal of chicken coops. He’s got electric doors for them, and he’s got cameras so he can watch them. And, you know, he’s named them all. So he’s having a lot of fun.”
Then there’s star power that keeps egg farming in the public eye. Actor Jennifer Garner, entrepreneur Martha Stewart, and former soccer star David Beckham are among the notable backyard chicken owners. As were Meghan Markle and Prince Harry, who had a rescue-chicken coop at their Montecito, California, home, named for their son, “Archie’s Chick Inn.” When the family returned to Britain in August, the hens remained behind.
While backyard coops may be trendy, they actually hark back to the early 20th century, when farmers throughout the U.S. raised chickens both for family meals and for sale to local groceries.
Mechanization moves
By the 1960s, automation kicked in, and commercial farms began to take over.
Instead of hens scratching in the dirt, they roosted in elevated cages. Conveyor belts transported eggs to be washed, inspected via camera and acoustic crack detectors, and packed by robots into cartons. These days, most chicken eggs aren’t touched by a human hand until a consumer opens the carton.
Today’s typical commercial operation might have 1 million or more hens. Chip-in Farm has 3,000. In 1970, the farm was preparing to make the switch to automation. But the Couvees’ grandfather died before that transition could take place. The farm’s flock dwindled to almost nothing. Neil, a recent high school graduate, kept the operation going by putting out fresh eggs in the shop each day and using an honor-system cash box.
When his older brother, Paul, graduated from college, the pair decided to expand the shop’s inventory. Today it offers cans of Campbell’s soup, Pepperidge Farm cookies, fresh produce (mostly from nearby farms), and, of course, eggs kept in the same cooler their grandfather used.
“People say all the time that you can tell the difference” in taste between a commercial and a farm-fresh egg, says Paul Couvee.
He recalls visiting his girlfriend’s family and bringing along some fresh eggs to cook. She was skeptical, he says. But “her father couldn’t stop talking about them.” He chuckles at the story of his future wife. “I think that’s why she married me: for the eggs.”
